I am 65 years old, and I have farmed this same 4.5 mu of land in Quzhou County for 40 years. I finished high school, so I can read fertilizer labels myself, do the nutrient sums in my head, and I keep a small account book where I record every jin of seed and every kilowatt-hour for the well pump. Last year my wheat made about 480 kg per mu and my maize made about 580 kg per mu. This year I want to push both crops up a step, but I will not gamble — on a farm this small, every 50 kg bag of compound fertilizer is real money out of my pocket, and a failed crop would be a real disaster. My son works in a factory in Handan city and sends some cash home, but the grain from this land is still the backbone of my household.

It is early October now, so I am busy with the winter wheat. I will run the rotary tiller over the maize stubble to break up the ground, then sow an improved wheat variety at 17 kg per mu. Before sowing, I spread 50 kg per mu of 16-16-16 compound fertilizer as my base dressing — that gives me exactly 8 kg of nitrogen, 8 kg of phosphorus, and 8 kg of potassium per mu. I know the soil here is loamy alluvial soil and fairly decent, but after four decades of wheat and maize the phosphorus gets drawn down every year, so I make sure the base fertilizer carries plenty. Next March, at the jointing stage, I will topdress 15 kg per mu of urea, which adds another 6.9 kg of nitrogen. I will irrigate three times using my well: once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, once at jointing, and once at grain filling in mid-May. The electricity bill is my own money, so I do not waste water, but skipping irrigation on wheat is false economy. For crop protection, I spray herbicide once in early spring and fungicide once at heading — two applications in total.

Next June, right after I cut the wheat, I will plant hybrid maize seed at 2.5 kg per mu using no-tillage direct seeding. The summer season is short here, and saving three days between wheat harvest and maize sowing matters if I want the grain to mature before autumn frost. At sowing, I put 40 kg per mu of 20-10-10 compound fertilizer in the furrow, and at the big trumpet stage I topdress with 15 kg per mu of urea. That comes to 14.9 kg of nitrogen, 4 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu. Maize is hungry for nitrogen when the ears are forming, and splitting the application keeps the plants from going short at the critical moment. I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing if the weather has been dry, and once at tasseling. Two pesticide sprays — herbicide at the three-leaf stage, and insecticide when I start seeing corn borers in the whorl.

I already walked around the village and checked what my neighbors are buying. Most families are using similar fertilizer rates. I thought about trimming 5 kg off the compound fertilizer to save a few yuan, but then I remembered what happened to Old Wang three years ago when he tried to save on fertilizer — his ears were half empty and he lost more money than he saved. On 4.5 mu, I would rather apply a little too much than risk a bad harvest. This plan is almost the same as what I did last year, with just a touch more nitrogen on the maize because last year's ears were slightly smaller than I wanted.
